marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q015.takeaway: Posterior limb of internal capsule is supplied by MCA lenticulostriate, anterior choroidal and PCA posterolateral branches, not Heubner artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q015.displayText: The marked posterior limb of the internal capsule is supplied by Charcot (lenticulostriate) branches of the middle cerebral artery, anterior choroidal artery from internal carotid artery, and posterolateral branches of posterior cerebral artery. Recurrent artery of Heubner is not among these sources. The source figure labels internal-capsule regions and their arterial territories.
emphasis: posterior limb of the internal capsule

rationales.a: MCA lenticulostriate (Charcot) arteries supply the posterior limb, so MCA is part of its supply.
rationales.c: Anterior choroidal artery from ICA supplies the posterior limb, so this is not the exception.
rationales.d: Posterolateral PCA branches also contribute to posterior-limb supply; recurrent artery of Heubner does not.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q016.takeaway: Putamen does not receive a direct supply from the posterior communicating artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q016.displayText: Posterior communicating artery does not supply putamen. The source image depicts the lentiform nucleus and adjacent deep structures; putamen receives striate and choroidal contributions rather than posterior communicating artery supply.
emphasis: Posterior communicating artery does not supply putamen

rationales.a: Medial striate branches contribute to deep basal-ganglia perfusion; posterior communicating artery is not a putamen supply.
rationales.b: Lateral striate (lenticulostriate) branches of MCA supply putamen and adjacent basal ganglia.
rationales.c: Anterior choroidal artery supplies portions of basal ganglia including posterior putamen; PCom is the excluded vessel.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q017.takeaway: Superior cerebral (bridging) veins drain into the superior sagittal sinus.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q017.displayText: A crescent-shaped hyperdense collection indicates acute subdural hematoma from torn bridging cerebral veins, often superior cerebral veins. Superior cerebral veins drain into superior sagittal sinus. Superficial cerebral veins drain cortex; deep cerebral veins drain deep structures. Superior cerebral veins drain superior superolateral and medial surfaces to superior sagittal sinus. Inferior cerebral veins drain inferior hemisphere to transverse, superior petrosal, cavernous and sphenoparietal sinuses, and some to inferior sagittal sinus. Superficial middle cerebral vein drains lateral surface and empties into cavernous sinus. Internal cerebral veins begin near foramen of Monro and unite as great cerebral vein; basal veins also drain into great cerebral vein, which passes beneath corpus callosum and joins straight sinus.

rationales.a: Great cerebral vein is a deep vein formed from internal cerebral veins and drains to straight sinus, not from superficial bridging veins.
rationales.b: Vein of Galen drains deep structures and basal veins to straight sinus.
rationales.d: Inferior sagittal sinus receives some inferior cerebral veins but not the superior cerebral bridging veins described.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q018.takeaway: Superficial middle cerebral vein drains to cavernous sinus and communicates with sagittal and transverse sinuses.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q018.displayText: Superficial middle cerebral vein lies in lateral sulcus and drains much of lateral cerebral hemisphere. It empties into cavernous sinus. It connects to superior sagittal sinus through superior anastomotic vein of Trolard and to transverse sinus through inferior anastomotic vein of Labbé.

rationales.a: Transverse sinus is reached via inferior anastomotic vein of Labbé, not direct termination of superficial middle cerebral vein.
rationales.c: Superior sagittal sinus connects by superior anastomotic vein of Trolard; direct drainage is cavernous sinus.
rationales.d: Straight sinus drains deep venous system and great cerebral vein, not superficial middle cerebral vein.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q019.takeaway: Internal cerebral veins unite to form the great cerebral vein of Galen.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q019.displayText: Two internal cerebral veins join below the splenium of corpus callosum to form the great cerebral vein (vein of Galen). It receives basal veins and drains into straight sinus.

rationales.a: Anterior cerebral vein is not the deep confluence formed by two internal cerebral veins.
rationales.b: Middle cerebral veins are superficial cortical drainage; the joined deep veins form great cerebral vein.
rationales.d: Inferior cerebral veins are superficial channels draining inferior hemisphere, not the vein formed beneath splenium.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q020.takeaway: Great cerebral vein drains into straight sinus.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q020.displayText: The great cerebral vein of Galen drains into the straight sinus. The source figure shows the cerebral venous drainage pattern.

rationales.a: Inferior petrosal sinus drains cavernous sinus, not great cerebral vein.
rationales.c: Sigmoid sinus receives transverse sinus and continues to internal jugular vein.
rationales.d: Occipital sinus is a posterior dural sinus and is not the direct terminus of vein of Galen.
